details:
**Sawm and Ramadan**
Sawm is the Islamic fast and the fourth of the Five Pillars of Islam. During Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, adult Muslims abstain from food, drink, and sexual relations from dawn to sunset; the Qur'an (Al-Baqara 2:183) says fasting "is prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you" so that believers may gain piety (taqwa).

**Suhoor and iftar**
The two meals framing each day of the Ramadan fast. Suhoor is eaten before dawn and the fajr prayer, and iftar breaks the fast at sunset, traditionally beginning with dates and water or milk, following the example of Muhammad.

**Eid al-Fitr**
The "Festival of Breaking the Fast," celebrated on the first day of Shawwal when the new moon marks the end of Ramadan. Fasting is forbidden on this day, which is marked by prayers, sweets, and charity.

**Yom Kippur**
The Jewish Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the High Holy Days, on which Jews fast for about 25 hours while praying for repentance. It is the only fast commanded in the Torah (Leviticus 23:26-32) and the only fast that takes place even on Shabbat.

**Tisha B'Av**
The ninth of the Hebrew month of Av, considered the saddest day of the Jewish calendar, observed with a full fast. It mourns the destruction of the First and Second Temples in Jerusalem, among other disasters.

**Sallekhana (Santhara)**
The Jain practice of gradually fasting to death at the end of one's life, undertaken when a person has no remaining responsibilities, as a way to shed karma. The Mauryan emperor Chandragupta Maurya is said to have died this way; it was briefly banned by an Indian court in 2015 before the Supreme Court stayed the ban. Jains also practice lesser fasts, especially during the festival of Paryushana.

**Lent**
The forty-day Christian season of penance before Easter, beginning on Ash Wednesday, which commemorates Jesus fasting for forty days in the desert while being tempted by Satan. Catholics are required to fast and abstain from meat on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and many give up a luxury for the season.

**Baha'i Nineteen-Day Fast**
Baha'is fast from sunrise to sunset during the 19-day month of Ala, the last month of the Baha'i calendar, which immediately precedes the new year festival of Naw-Ruz at the spring equinox.

**Karva Chauth**
A one-day Hindu festival, observed mainly in northern India, on which married women fast from sunrise until moonrise to pray for the safety and long life of their husbands.

**Ta'anit and minor Jewish fasts**
Ta'anit is the Hebrew term for a fast. Besides Yom Kippur and Tisha B'Av, Jews observe minor fasts such as the Fast of Gedaliah (mourning the assassination of the governor Gedaliah), Asara B'Tevet, the Seventeenth of Tammuz, the Fast of Esther the day before Purim, and the Fast of the Firstborn on the day before Passover.

**Fidya and kaffara**
Compensations in Islam for fasts missed during Ramadan. Fidya is paid by those who cannot fast at all, such as the chronically ill or elderly, while kaffara is the penalty for deliberately breaking a Ramadan fast, such as by intercourse, requiring 60 consecutive days of fasting or feeding 60 poor people.

**The Buddha and Sujata**
Before his enlightenment, Siddhartha Gautama practiced extreme fasting until he nearly died, an episode depicted in famous emaciated "Fasting Buddha" sculptures from Gandhara. He abandoned extreme asceticism for the Middle Way after accepting a bowl of milk-rice from a village woman named Sujata.

**Voluntary fasts in Islam and the "shield" hadith**
A hadith narrated by Abu Hurayrah and collected by al-Bukhari calls fasting a "shield" against sin and hellfire. Muslims are encouraged to fast voluntarily on days such as Ashura and the Day of Arafah, and for six days in Shawwal, the month after Ramadan.

**Black fast**
An especially strict form of fasting, abstaining from all food (and in some forms all drink) for a period, practiced by some Pentecostals and historically in Christian penitential traditions. A related practice is the "Daniel fast," limited to vegetables and pulses, modeled on the Book of Daniel.

**Mormon fast Sunday**
Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints fast on the first Sunday of each month and donate the money they would have spent on those meals as a "fast offering" to help the poor.
